title: Order of Draw & Tubes
body:
## The order and why

CLSI order for venipuncture. The whole point is to stop one tube's additive from riding into the next one on the needle.

1. **Blood cultures / sterile (yellow SPS)** — sterility can only be lost, never regained
2. **Light blue (sodium citrate)** — coags are ruined by carryover of clot activator or heparin
3. **Red / gold SST (serum)** — clot activator here would have contaminated the blue
4. **Green (heparin)**
5. **Lavender / pink (EDTA)** — EDTA chelates calcium and carries potassium; a trace in a chemistry tube falsely raises `K` and falsely drops `Ca`
6. **Gray (fluoride/oxalate)** — last, because fluoride poisons most other assays

> **Key:** Out-of-order draws do not look wrong. They just produce a believable, wrong number. That is why the order is memorized, not reasoned out each time.

## Tube table

| Color | Additive | Inversions | Common tests | Fill rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Yellow (SPS) | Sodium polyanethol sulfonate | `8–10` | Blood cultures | To the fill line on the bottle |
| Light blue | `3.2%` sodium citrate | `3–4` | PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer, factor assays | **Must fill completely** — `9:1` blood-to-citrate. Under about `90%` fill, the result is rejected |
| Red (plastic) | Clot activator | `5` | Chemistry, serology, blood bank, drug levels | Standard fill; clot `30 min` before spinning |
| Gold / tiger SST | Clot activator + gel separator | `5` | CMP, BMP, lipids, most chemistry | Clot fully upright `30 min` before centrifuge |
| Orange | Thrombin (rapid serum) | `5–8` | STAT chemistry, troponin at some sites | Clots in about `5 min` |
| Green | Sodium or lithium heparin | `8` | Plasma chemistry, ammonia, lactate, chromosome studies | Standard |
| Light green PST | Lithium heparin + gel | `8` | STAT chemistry, electrolytes | Standard |
| Lavender / purple | K2 or K3 EDTA | `8–10` | CBC with differential, ESR, HbA1c, reticulocyte count | Fill to the line — underfill shrinks cells and falsely lowers hematocrit |
| Pink | K2 EDTA | `8–10` | Type and screen, crossmatch | Full fill, and blood-bank labeling rules are stricter |
| Royal blue | EDTA or none | `8–10` | Trace metals, toxicology, zinc, copper | Special low-metal tube |
| Gray | Sodium fluoride / potassium oxalate | `8–10` | Glucose (preserved), lactate, ethanol | Fluoride stops glycolysis, so glucose stays honest for hours |
| Tan | Sodium heparin or EDTA, lead-free | `8–10` | Lead |

Minimum volume varies by manufacturer and tube size — most adult tubes want at least `2–3 mL`, pediatric microtainers `250–500 microliters`. Read the fill line, not a memorized number.

## Blood cultures

- A **set** is one aerobic plus one anaerobic bottle. Standard workup is `2` sets from `2` separate venipuncture sites, drawn **before** antibiotics.
- **Volume is everything.** Adults: `8–10 mL` per bottle, `20 mL` per set. Under-filled bottles are the top cause of false negatives. Pediatric volume is weight-based, often `1–4 mL` total.
- **Prep:** scrub the bottle tops with `70%` alcohol and let dry. Scrub the skin with chlorhexidine-alcohol for `30 s` and air-dry `30 s` (povidone-iodine needs `1.5–2 min`). Do not re-palpate the site after prep unless you re-glove and re-prep.
- **Bottle order:** with a **syringe**, fill the **anaerobic** bottle first (air collects at the top of a syringe and would go into the anaerobic bottle last-in). With a **winged/butterfly set drawn straight into bottles**, fill the **aerobic** bottle first, because the air in the tubing gets pushed into whichever bottle is first.
- Prefer peripheral sticks. If you must draw from a line, pair it with a peripheral set and label which is which.

## IV catheter gauges

| Gauge | Color | Typical flow | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `14 G` | Orange | about `300 mL/min` | Massive transfusion, major trauma |
| `16 G` | Gray | about `200 mL/min` | Trauma, surgery, rapid volume |
| `18 G` | Green | about `100 mL/min` | Blood products, CT contrast, OR |
| `20 G` | Pink | about `60 mL/min` | General adult, contrast, most blood |
| `22 G` | Blue | about `35 mL/min` | Elderly, fragile veins, pediatrics |
| `24 G` | Yellow | about `20 mL/min` | Neonates, infants |

Flow rates are approximate and depend on catheter length and brand.

## Hemolysis prevention

- Use `21–23 G`; avoid `25 G` and smaller for tubes
- Tourniquet on for under `1 minute`; release once blood flows
- Let alcohol dry completely before the stick
- Draw below an IV site or from the opposite arm — never above a running line
- No fist pumping
- Do not pull a syringe plunger hard, and never force blood through the needle into a tube
- Fill tubes to the line and invert **gently** the stated number of times — do not shake
- Transport promptly; check whether your lab allows the pneumatic tube for that test

## Specimen rejection reasons

Unlabeled or mislabeled tube; two-identifier mismatch; wrong tube type; clotted EDTA specimen; quantity not sufficient (QNS); hemolysis; short-filled citrate; expired tube; contaminated with IV fluid; wrong transport temperature; excessive transport delay.

## Specimens that go on ice

Ammonia, lactate (unless in a gray fluoride tube), blood gases held more than about `30 min`, pyruvate, gastrin, parathyroid hormone, homocysteine, renin, ACTH, catecholamines. Protect bilirubin, vitamin A and B6, carotene and porphyrins **from light** instead.

> **On shift:** Two identifiers — full name plus date of birth or medical record number. Never the room number. Ask the patient to *state* their name and date of birth, match it to the armband and the order, then label the tubes **at the bedside, in the patient's presence, before you leave the room**. Name, date, time, and your initials.
